questions.prompt: Where must legacy `#include <vector>` directives appear inside a module interface file?
options: Between `module;` and `export module M;` inside the global module fragment.
Immediately after `export module M;` inside the module purview.
Inside `export { #include <vector> }` so callers receive `std::vector`.
Inside `module :private;` at the end of the file.
questions.explanation: Including a header after `export module M;` attaches all of its declarations to module M, conflicting with other units that include `<vector>` in the global module. Placing `#include` in the global module fragment (`module;`) keeps those declarations in the global module.

questions.prompt: What happens to a `#define DEBUG_TAG 1` macro written inside a named module interface unit `export module app;`?
options: It leaks to importers if placed after `export module app;`.
It is exported only if written as `export #define DEBUG_TAG 1`.
It never leaks to importers of `app`, because named modules do not export preprocessor macros.
It causes a compile error because `#define` is forbidden inside any module unit.
questions.explanation: Named modules expose semantic declarations, never preprocessor state. Unlike `#include` or header units (`import <h>;`), macros defined in a named module never affect importing translation units.

questions.prompt: Given module `demo` below, which statement in `main.cpp` compiles cleanly?
options: Box b = make_box();
auto b = make_box(); int y = b.x;
export Box b = make_box();
Neither `Box` nor `b.x` can be used because `Box` is not exported.
questions.explanation: Although `Box` is not exported—making its name invisible to unqualified lookup (`Box b` fails)—`Box` is reachable because exported `make_box()` returns it ([module.reach]). Therefore `auto b = make_box();` and accessing `b.x` are well-formed.

questions.prompt: Why does writing `import math:core;` directly inside `main.cpp` (a non-module consumer file) fail to compile?
options: Because module partitions must be named with `::` instead of `:`.
Because module partitions can only be imported by translation units belonging to the same module `math`.
Because partitions cannot contain exported functions.
Because `main.cpp` must declare `module math;` before importing any module.
questions.explanation: Under [module.import], a module-partition import (`import :core;`) has no module name prefix and is valid only inside translation units of the owning module. External consumers import the primary module (`import math;`), which uses `export import :core;` to expose interface partitions.

questions.prompt: Why is an `export inline` function inside module `M` ill-formed if it calls a `static` helper function declared in `M`'s purview?
options: Because `static` gives `secret` internal linkage (making it TU-local), and an exported inline entity cannot expose TU-local entities.
Because `inline` functions are forbidden inside C++20 module interfaces.
Because `static` functions in a module purview automatically receive external linkage and clash across units.
Because `api()` must be declared `constexpr` to call non-exported helpers.
questions.explanation: In [basic.link], entities with internal linkage (such as namespace-scope `static` functions or unnamed-namespace declarations) are translation-unit-local. Exposing a TU-local entity from a non-TU-local inline function or template is ill-formed; dropping `static` gives `secret()` module linkage instead.

questions.prompt: In `int module = 3; int import = module + 1;` inside a regular function body, how does the lexer classify `module` and `import`?
options: Syntax error, because `module` and `import` became hard keywords in C++20.
Valid only when compiled without `-std=c++20`.
Valid only if placed inside `module :private;`.
Valid identifiers, because `module` and `import` are identifiers with special meaning only in module/import directive positions.
questions.explanation: To preserve backward compatibility with existing C++ codebases using `module` or `import` as variable, parameter, or field names, C++20 made them identifiers with special meaning ([lex.name]) recognized only at the start of module-declarations and import-declarations.
